title: Account Manipulation: Additional Email Delegate Permissions
shortTitle: Account Manipulation: Additional Email Delegate Permissions
summary: This sub-technique of account manipulation is about giving a second account the right to read or send mail as the first one. In on-premises Exchange and in the hosted Exchange service this is done with mailbox permission and delegation cmdlets, and it can also be done through administration consoles. In Google Workspace, delegation is configured in the admin console or by the mailbox owner in their mail settings. A more granular form assigns folder level permissions or roles, for example granting the default or anonymous user rights over the root of the mailbox or over the inbox, which lets any account in the tenant reach the target's mail folders. The value to an adversary is durability and visibility: shared mailboxes are legitimate features, so a delegated account can read mail, watch for replies to a campaign, or send messages from a trusted address that spam filters are unlikely to question. Detection focuses on the permission change itself: administrative audit records for delegation and folder permission changes, mailbox access by an identity that does not normally read that mailbox, and mail that was sent by an account whose sign-in activity does not match the sending behaviour.

beginner.definition: This is a sub-technique of account manipulation, and it means an attacker gives another mailbox permission to open or send from the victim's mailbox. The second account may be a normal user account the attacker already controls. Because the permission is stored in the mail system, it keeps working after the victim changes their password.
beginner.whyItMatters: Mail holds password resets, invoices and private conversations, so reading it is very valuable. A delegated account can also send mail that looks completely genuine, which makes phishing much harder to spot. These permissions are easy to forget, and many tenants never review who can read whose mailbox.
howItWorks: The attacker gets control of an account that can change mailbox settings, usually an administrator.
They grant another account full access or send-as rights over the target mailbox.
Alternatively they set folder permissions so that any account in the company can read the inbox.
The attacker then reads mail, looking for finance, password or project information.
They may also send messages from the trusted mailbox to colleagues, so the mail passes filters.
The mail system writes an audit record naming the actor, the target mailbox and the permission.
beginner.example: Think of an office where the post room sorts mail into pigeonholes. A manager quietly adds a colleague's name to your pigeonhole label, so that person can take your letters and post new ones in your name. Everything looks normal at the post room, and the letters still carry your handwriting on the envelope.
takeaways: Review mailbox delegation and folder permissions regularly, not only after an incident.
An administrator account that reads mail it has no business reason to read is a strong signal.
Mail sent by a signed-in user from an odd location deserves a closer look.

objectives: Explain how this sub-technique differs from the parent account manipulation technique.
Describe the behaviours it covers, including mailbox delegation and folder level permissions.
Identify the audit records that capture mailbox permission changes.
Distinguish legitimate shared mailbox use from malicious delegation.
Explain how delegated access supports later phishing and information theft.
